claims.title: How can one coefficient select a single place above q?
claims.hypotheses: The coefficient ring is the ring of integers of a number field. A maximal ideal above q has ramification index r and positive residue degree f.
claims.statement: There is an integral element congruent to one at the chosen prime power 𝔴^(rf) and zero at the complementary factor to power f. Modulo q it projects onto the full local factor C/𝔴^r.

claims.title: Which integral products connect the local parameter to Frobenius?
claims.hypotheses: The local integral projector has been chosen modulo q^f and the other prime powers have product 𝔟.
claims.statement: There is an integral parameter a of valuation one at 𝔴 with a(1−e)=q^f s and d=e a^(r−1). Then ad=qc and c is a unit on the chosen component, so c′ce=e modulo q.

claims.title: What are the two annihilators in the coefficient ring?
claims.hypotheses: In C/(q), e selects the 𝔴-primary component and a,d are the two complementary local powers.
claims.statement: The projection of the residue ideal is aS. The annihilator of d is aS+(1−e)S, and the annihilator of a is dS+(1−e)S.

claims.title: What do the projector and its annihilators look like above 2?
claims.hypotheses: Let F=ℚ(√2,(1+√−7)/2), with 𝔴 over 2 on which β=(1+√−7)/2 reduces to one.
claims.statement: The quotient of the integer ring by 2 is a product of two dual-number rings over 𝔽₂. The two local coefficients both reduce to (η,0). For x=(η,1+η) the projected equation has eight witnesses and the full decomposition has 32.

claims.title: When do the two coefficient-kernel formulas survive on a module?
claims.hypotheses: The identities e²=e, ed=d and ad=0 and the two ring kernel formulas hold in C/qC. Here k is a field of characteristic q and M is projective over k⊗ℤC.
claims.statement: On M the kernel of d equals aM+(1−e)M, and the e-projection of the kernel of a equals dM.

claims.title: Why do the coefficient-kernel formulas hold on primitive de Rham cohomology?
claims.hypotheses: At the geometric point of the degree-one unitary datum the crystalline lift and the de Rham comparison hold. The level is at least three and prime to q.
claims.statement: The two annihilator identities hold for the action on primitive first de Rham cohomology. A crystalline lift gives projectivity on the dual, and the identities on cohomology follow by annihilating subspaces.

claims.title: How can one compute ideal torsion using a single endomorphism?
claims.hypotheses: I is a nonzero integral ideal of a number field and q is a rational prime.
claims.statement: There are a nonzero g, an ideal J prime to I and (q), and t in I with IJ=(g) and 1−t in J. The ideals I and J are generated by (g,t) and (g,1−t), respectively.

claims.title: Why does the ideal-torsion group have rank equal to a power of the ideal norm?
claims.hypotheses: The marked unitary abelian scheme has a coefficient action, geometric level identifications away from q, and an integral lattice of rank mn[F:ℚ] over ℤ. The ideal I is nonzero.
claims.statement: The group killed by I is finite flat of constant rank Nm(I)^(mn). The coprime decomposition of principal torsion is an isomorphism over the base.

claims.title: How can one coefficient measure a simultaneous character space?
claims.hypotheses: A finite-dimensional representation of the integer coefficient ring over an algebraically closed residue field has each characteristic polynomial equal to a fixed h-th power of the regular one.
claims.statement: For each labelled character, the dimension of its simultaneous generalized eigenspace equals h times the corresponding dimension in the regular representation.

claims.title: Why do Frobenius-conjugate character spaces have the same dimension?
claims.hypotheses: In the degree-one marked unitary datum at a geometric point, the de Rham characteristic polynomial agrees with the reduction of the one obtained from the auxiliary Tate marking. The residue field is perfect.
claims.statement: The simultaneous generalized eigenspaces for χ and its q-power iterates have equal dimension in primitive de Rham cohomology.
